extracted.intended_audience: patent classifiers, patent examiners, patent searchers, and other intellectual property office staff using the IPC
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and procedural guidance for assigning IPC classification symbols and indexing codes to patent documents, selecting subclass/groups, handling combinations/subcombinations, and preparing/searching fields of search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate classification of each disclosed subject and subcombination
rubrics_metrics.description: Each distinct subject of the invention disclosed in the patent document is to be classified separately; if a subcombination of the subject of the invention is novel and non-obvious itself, it is separately classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is the general rule used in the subclass to separately apply classification for each subject. Subcombinations not selected for main classification should be considered for classification as additional information (see paragraphs on subcombinations and additional information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common rule (default) — single place principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The common rule is the default classification rule in the IPC, based on the principle of devising the Classification so that one and the same technical subject can be classified in one and the same place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle assumes classification places are mutually exclusive; when not mutually exclusive, apply the principles of paragraph 144(b). No general priority rules apply in common rule areas, but certain priority principles (paragraph 142) can be used to limit unnecessary multiple classification and to select groups that adequately represent the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority principles for common rule areas
rubrics_metrics.description: In common rule areas, the following principles may be applied to limit unnecessary multiple classification: (a) groups for more complex matter take priority over groups for less complex matter; (b) groups for more specialised subject matter take priority over groups for less specialised subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: combinations take priority over subcombinations; 'whole things' take priority over 'details'; unique types or matter with means for solving particular problems take priority over general groups. These principles form the basis for the standardised sequence of main groups. However, priority should not be applied between groups covering different aspects (e.g., function vs application) in common rule areas — classification should be made in all appropriate places. References or local precedence rules overrule these general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple classification when subject has several aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying subject matter characterised by several aspects or when assigning additional classification symbols representing useful information for searching, principles of multiple classification apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multiple classification to represent different aspects or additional useful search information (see paragraphs 102–107 references). Consider additional symbols for aspects useful in Boolean searching or other search strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for identifying detailed classification place after subclass selection
rubrics_metrics.description: After selecting the appropriate subclass, identify a detailed classification place starting at main group level by (a) reviewing all groups to see if only one provides for the subject; (b) if two or more groups provide for it, use priority principles; (c) repeat at each hierarchical level until no further subgroup provides for the technical subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two or more groups provide, and priority principles indicate a priority, the priority group must be selected; other lower-priority groups may also be selected if useful for search purposes, applying step (c) separately for each selected group. If priority cannot be determined, apply step (c) separately for each group. Repeat steps at each indentation level until the deepest appropriate subgroup is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of combinations when no specific place exists (common rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no specific place for a combination is provided in a common-rule area, classify the combination according to its subcombinations, following the priority principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcombinations not selected for primary classification should be considered for classification as additional information. Apply paragraph 142 principles when choosing which subcombinations to classify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas with priority classification rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain areas the IPC applies priority classification rules that give general priority between all groups in that area to improve consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These schemes are specially adapted; even though general priority rules apply, multiple classification is still possible when necessary. Areas with priority rules are clearly marked by a note at the highest place covered by such rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: First place priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the first place priority rule applies, classification is made in the first appropriate place at each hierarchical level (in absence of indication to the contrary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: determine the first main group in the subclass providing at least in part for the subject; then the first one-dot subgroup providing at least in part for the subject; repeat through successive indentation levels until the first subgroup at the deepest subgroup level is determined. For combinations lacking specific place, classify in the first group that provides for at least one subcombination. Novel subcombinations must also be separately classified following the same procedure. Subcombinations useful for search may be added as additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Last place priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the last place priority rule applies, classification is made in the last appropriate place at each hierarchical level (in absence of indication to the contrary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure analogous to first place rule but selecting the last main group, then last one-dot subgroup, repeating until the last subgroup at the deepest subgroup level is determined. If no specific place for a combination, classify in the last group that provides for at least one subcombination. Novel subcombinations must also be separately classified following this rule. Subcombinations useful for search may be added as additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rules override general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In limited places, special classification rules override the general classification rules; where used they are clearly specified in notes at the places concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Note 2(b) following the title of subclass C08L specifies that compositions are classified according to the macromolecular constituent(s) present in the highest proportion; if equal proportions, classify according to each constituent. Follow explicit special-rule notes where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of classification symbols and indexing codes on patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The order on patent documents should be: (1) classification symbols representing invention information — the symbol which most adequately represents the invention listed first; (2) classification symbols representing additional information; (3) indexing codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification symbols and indexing codes are presented in tabular form in one or more columns, with only one symbol or code on each line. The invention information symbol that most adequately represents the invention should be listed first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and typographical conventions for IPC symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying using the core level, IPC symbols are in regular font (non-italics); when using advanced level, IPC symbols are in italics. Invention information symbols are printed/displayed in bold; additional information symbols in regular (non-bold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If classified partly using core level, place the current version indicator of the core level (year) in round brackets after the abbreviation 'Int.Cl.' When using advanced level, include version indicator (year, month) in round brackets after each IPC symbol to indicate when the symbol was created or substantially revised at the advanced level. Examples in paragraphs 161(a)-(c) illustrate combinations of advanced/core listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special residual classification places for new/uncovered subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When invention information is not adequately covered by any subclass of the most appropriate section, classify it in the special residual main group of that section designated '99Z 99/00' for the section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each special residual main group has title 'Subject matter not otherwise provided for in this section.' Residual main groups in subclasses are placed at the end of the subclass and designated 99/00 where necessary. Before using a residual main group, consider classification in other subclasses or main groups and give due respect to procedures for borderline/classification elsewhere. Do not classify combinations covered by two or more different main groups in a residual main group unless indicated otherwise. If no residual main group exists in the subclass, classify in the section-level special residual main group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of searches using IPC symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: IPC may be used for various kinds of searches: (a) Novelty Search — determine novelty vs prior art; (b) Patentability/Validity Search — locate documents relevant to novelty and other criteria like inventive step; (c) Infringement Search — find patents/published applications that might be infringed; (d) Informative (state-of-the-art) Search — familiarise with state of the art and identify existing patent publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability/Validity searches should cover all technical fields that may contain material pertinent to the invention. Informative searches provide background, alternatives, and licensing evaluation information. Choose search type based on objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing for a search — establish and express technical subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Before searching, clearly establish the technical subject(s) of the search and identify proper IPC place(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate a clear statement of the technical subject and identify technical terms that cover broadly or specifically the field. For Patentability Searches, more than one technical subject may need to be searched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining a field of search — use Catchword Index and IPC tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Catchword Index to the IPC or IPC:CLASS CD-ROM to search for technical terms in the text of the IPC; this may indicate a precise group or at least a main group/subclass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Catchword Index should not be read as modifying any part of the IPC. If Catchword Index or CD-ROM does not yield a pertinent field, scan the eight IPC sections and class/subclass titles, then inspect subclass titles and definitions. Use the subclass index for quick navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative subclass identification via text search and statistical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If index-based navigation is insufficient, determine appropriate subclass by text searching databases of patent documents and performing statistical analysis of classification symbols that appear in retrieved documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subclasses that most often appear in classification symbols of retrieved documents should be considered for inclusion in the field of search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the most indented (deepest) appropriate group for search
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining the appropriate main group, scan its one-dot subgroups and select the most indented (i.e., with most dots) subgroup that is most appropriate to the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the chosen group includes a precedence reference to another group, search the precedence group as well. After completing the search in the chosen group, consider hierarchically higher (less indented) groups under which it is indented to capture wider subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling precedence references between groups
rubrics_metrics.description: When a chosen group includes a precedence reference (e.g., '7/16 (7/12 takes precedence)'), it may be necessary to search the group taking precedence as well as the chosen group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example C08F 2/04 vs 2/32: polymerisation in solution (2/32 takes precedence) and polymerisation in water-in-oil emulsions — polymerisation characterised by taking place in a particular solvent may be found in either place; search both places unless the subject cannot take place in the precedence place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching strategy in areas with multiple classification or hybrid systems
rubrics_metrics.description: In areas where multiple classification is applied or hybrid systems exist, first use a combination of classification symbols or classification symbols plus indexing codes to make a specific search query; broaden afterwards with the most pertinent classification symbols alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps obtain complete results while keeping the initial query specific; subsequently broaden to ensure completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterate when search fails to retrieve pertinent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to retrieve pertinent documents may indicate the proper IPC place has not been located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When this occurs, re-express the technical subject differently and reconsider the field-of-search procedure (re-run catchword/index scans, subclass checks, text searches, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master Classification Database (MCD) use and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The MCD is a bibliographic database storing bibliographic data elements (including IPC symbols) of patent documents at various publication levels and family information; during IPC reform it was used for storing allotted IPC symbols and updating them after scheme revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MCD stores documents classified according to current core and updated advanced levels, enabling searches using only current Classification. Copies or indirect access to MCD data are possible via WIPO/office websites or commercial hosts. It facilitates searches using IPC symbols, applicant/inventor names, titles, abstracts, priorities and family information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: invention information and use of claims for guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention information comprises all novel and unobvious subject matter in the total disclosure (description, drawings, claims) that represents an addition to the state of the art; 'invention information' should usually be determined using the claims of the patent document for guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine invention information primarily by reference to the claims but consider the total disclosure in context of the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of combination and subcombination
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'combination' is a technical 'thing' as a whole consisting of two or more steps or components put together for a purpose; a 'subcombination' is a subset of those steps or components and may itself be novel and unobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a three-step manufacturing process is a combination; two consecutive steps are a subcombination; a subcombination that is novel/non-obvious should be classified separately. Terms are relative: what is a subcombination in one context may be a combination in another; subcombinations may consist of further subcombinations.
